notes.meaning: The group of young prophets told Elisha that their meeting place was much too small for them. Their numbers had grown under his faithful teaching and leadership. This shows how God was blessing their community with steady spiritual growth.

The students asked permission to go to the Jordan Valley where there were plenty of trees to cut timber. Each man was willing to do hard physical work to build a new place to stay. Elisha agreed and told them to go.
One of the students asked Elisha to come along with them on the journey. They loved their teacher, respected his guidance, and wanted his presence as they worked. Elisha gladly agreed to join them.
Elisha traveled with them to the Jordan River, and the men began cutting down trees. They worked hard together beside the wooded banks. Even prophets in training were not above doing manual labor.

While one student was chopping down a tree, the iron axe head slipped off its wooden handle and fell into the deep river. He cried out in distress because the axe was borrowed from a neighbor. Iron tools were rare and valuable, and he was too poor to pay for a replacement.

Elisha asked where the tool had dropped, and the man pointed out the exact spot. The prophet cut a stick, threw it into the water, and the heavy iron miraculously floated to the top. The stick had no natural power to lift iron, but God used it as a sign of His supernatural power.
Elisha told the young man to reach out and take the floating iron tool. The student reached his hand into the water and picked it up. God solved his problem, but still asked him to do his own part.

The king of Aram went to war against Israel and met with his military leaders to plan secret ambushes. He chose specific locations where he planned to set up camp and trap the Israelite army. Aram relied on surprise attacks and stealth rather than open battle.

God revealed the enemy's secret ambush plans to Elisha. The prophet sent a warning to the king of Israel to stay away from that exact spot because Syrian troops were waiting there. In this way, God protected the nation through His prophet.

The king of Israel sent scouts or troops to check the location Elisha warned about and secured the area. This happened multiple times, and the king was repeatedly saved from Syrian ambushes. God showed that no secret plan can be hidden from His sight.

The king of Aram became deeply angry and distressed when his plans kept failing. He gathered his officers and demanded to know which of them was secretly a spy for Israel. He assumed someone inside his own court was betraying him.

One of the king's officers explained that no Syrian was being disloyal. Instead, Elisha the prophet was telling the king of Israel the very words spoken in the king's private bedroom. The officer had likely heard of Elisha's miraculous gifts through the healing of Naaman.

The king ordered his men to scout out where Elisha was staying so he could capture him. When they reported that Elisha was in the town of Dothan, the king prepared his strike. He foolishly thought he could trap a prophet who could hear his most secret words.

The king sent a large force of horses, chariots, and troops to Dothan. They marched under cover of darkness and completely surrounded the town during the night. The Syrian king brought massive military power just to capture one unarmed man of God.

Elisha's servant woke up early in the morning and saw the town surrounded by enemy troops, horses, and war chariots. Overwhelmed by panic, the servant ran to Elisha and asked what they could possibly do. He saw only the visible danger and felt completely helpless.

Elisha told his servant not to be afraid because those on their side were far greater than the Syrian army. He knew that God's heavenly power always outmatches any human army. God's servants can rest in peace even when surrounded by trouble.

Elisha prayed for the Lord to open the young man's eyes so he could see reality as it truly was. God opened the servant's spiritual sight, and he saw the surrounding hills filled with fiery horses and chariots protecting Elisha. These fiery chariots were an army of angels sent by God to guard His prophet.

As the Syrian soldiers moved down toward him, Elisha prayed that God would strike the army with blindness. The Lord answered his prayer and struck them with a confusing blindness so they could not tell what was happening. God took away their ability to recognize him or understand their surroundings.

Elisha told the confused troops that they were on the wrong road and at the wrong city. He promised to lead them to the man they wanted, and he guided them about twelve miles south to the capital city of Samaria. He used a wartime strategy to lure the enemy into Israel's royal city without shedding blood.

Once they entered the gates of Samaria, Elisha prayed for God to open their eyes again. The Lord restored their clear sight, and the soldiers suddenly realized they were standing trapped inside the fortified capital of their enemy. God showed His absolute control over human perception.

When the king of Israel saw the helpless enemy army delivered into his hands, he eagerly asked Elisha twice if he should kill them. He called Elisha 'my father' out of sudden respect and excitement. The king wanted to slaughter the men who were now at his mercy.

Elisha forbade the king from harming the soldiers, explaining that they were prisoners brought there by God and not captured in his own battle. Instead of executing them, Elisha told the king to give them food and water and send them back to their master. God taught His people to show mercy and hospitality rather than cruelty to defeated enemies.

The king of Israel prepared a large feast for the Syrian soldiers, fed them well, and sent them peacefully on their way home. Because of this unexpected kindness and the wonder of God's power, Syrian raiding parties stopped invading Israel's territory for a time. Treating enemies with grace brought a season of peace.

Sometime later, King Ben-hadad of Aram gathered his whole army and marched against Israel to lay siege to Samaria. A siege meant surrounding the walled city completely so no food or supplies could get in or out. The peaceful pause had ended, and the city faced total cut-off.

The long siege caused a terrible famine inside Samaria. Food became so scarce that the head of a donkey—an unclean animal forbidden by the law of Moses—sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a small measure of dove's dung sold for five pieces of silver. People were desperate enough to spend huge sums of money on filthy and worthless scraps to survive.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars understand 'dove's dung' as a popular name for an inexpensive wild plant or seed pod rather than actual bird droppings.

notes.meaning: As the king of Israel walked along the city wall to inspect the defenses, a woman called out to him in agony, begging him for help. In times of national crisis, people naturally turned to the king as their supreme judge and protector. She hoped the royal court could solve her desperate plight.

The king answered bitterly that if the Lord would not rescue her, he had no way to help. He had no grain from the threshing floor and no wine from the presses to offer anyone. The king felt entirely powerless in the face of the famine.

When the king asked what the trouble was, the woman revealed a horrifying agreement. She and another woman had agreed to boil and eat her son one day, and eat the other woman's child the next day. The starvation had destroyed basic human affection.

The woman explained that they had cooked and eaten her child, but on the next day, the other woman hid her own son. This horrific scene fulfilled the ancient warnings in Deuteronomy about the curses that would follow rebellion against God. The tragedy showed how far the nation had fallen in its suffering.

When the king heard the gruesome story, he tore his royal garments in shock and grief. As he walked along the wall, the people could see that he was secretly wearing rough sackcloth next to his skin as a sign of mourning. Even with this outward sign of distress, his heart was not truly humbled before God.

The king swore a violent oath that God should strike him dead if he did not cut off Elisha's head before the day ended. Instead of repenting of his own sins and idolatry, the king blamed the prophet for the disaster. He treated God's messenger as the cause of Israel's misery.

Elisha was sitting in his house with the elders of the city when God revealed that the king had sent an executioner to behead him. Elisha warned the leaders that this 'son of a murderer' was coming and told them to bar the door against the messenger until the king arrived right behind him. Elisha called him the son of a murderer because King Joram's father Ahab had killed God's prophets and Naboth.

While Elisha was still speaking, the messenger arrived, followed closely by the king. The king declared that this terrible disaster had come from the Lord, so he saw no reason to wait for God's help any longer. In his despair and bitterness, the king was ready to give up on God entirely.
